utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please have the accused brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to be sure that the interpretation booths are ready and that all the parties hear me and will also hear the other judges. I turn first to my judges. Do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor hear? Does the Defence hear? Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, do you hear me? GENERAL BLASKIC: Good morning, your Honours. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to now have the appearances for the parties, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon. I will be representing the Prosecutor's Office this morning with my colleagues, to my right Mr. Andrew Cayley, to his right Mr. Gregory Kehoe. To my left is Mr. Emile van der Does de Willebois.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This constitution will be the same throughout the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARK HARMON
utterances.text: There may be one additional person and that is Mr. Douglas Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Turning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Russel Hayman. Together with my colleague Anto Nobilo we represent General Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, would you please rise? Very briefly I ask you to introduce yourself to the Tribunal, confirming who you are, how old you are, from what geographic area you come, where you had your residence at the time you came to the Hague, that is your residence in Croatia and your profession. This will be the only time which we will ask you these questions, but since the trial is now opening, I want to ask you these details. Would you please give them to us. GENERAL BLASKIC: Thank you, your Honours. My name is Tihomir Blaskic. I was born on 2nd November in Kiseljak in 1962. Before coming to the Hague I was living in Zagreb. My occupation is -- rather I graduated from the Military Academy of Ground Forces and I am a professional officer of the Croatian army by occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you married? Do you have children, Mr. Blaskic? GENERAL BLASKIC: Yes, I'm married since 1987. I have two children, a son called Dajan, nine years of age, and a son called Ivan of one year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. GENERAL BLASKIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask several preliminary questions at the time now that the trial of Tihomir Blaskic is beginning. First, I would like to turn to the Prosecution and ask that with the assistance of the registry that a single document relating to the amended indictment be indicated. I would like to recall to you that the indictment against General Blaskic was amended two times, not counting the original indictment, which had his name and six other names of accused. It was first amended in order to separate General Blaskic's case from the others, and then the indictment at the request of the Defence was modified concerning a certain number of points. What we like, myself and my colleagues, is a single document, which makes a definitive synthesis of the charges as they have been confirmed by the Tribunal be set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indictment which is now the second amended indictment charges General Blaskic -- it charges General Blaskic, your Honours, with 20 counts, three counts of crimes against humanity, six counts of grave breaches and 11 counts of violations of the laws or customs of war. The indictment, a copy of which I do not have in front of me, covers a substantial period of time and takes place in three municipalities, Busovaca municipality, the Vitez municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I am not asking you to begin that way. I have other preliminary points. I simply wanted to tell you that after the decision of the Tribunal on 23rd May 1997 we noted a certain number of changes after a discussion with both parties present and during that discussion we rendered the decision which confirms a certain number of charges. It tells you to go to Trial Chamber II, if necessary, to confirm certain other charges, and I would also like to recall that there was a new charge. What the Tribunal is asking is that following that decision we would like to have a single document which synthesises everything. It will be either you or the registry. I believe the Registry, according to what I was told by the Registry, is work being done now together with the Prosecutor. This is what the Tribunal is asking, that is the synthesis of the various decisions taken for the indictment be done. That is all I am asking for the time being. That is the point that the Tribunal wanted to stress, that is wanted to have that document. I would also like to recall, that is remind both of the parties, that this trial is opening today but that there are three types of decisions which are pending. They are preliminary decisions which might have some kind of repercussion on the conduct of the trial. Pending before Trial Chamber II, presided over by Judge McDonald, there is a dispute over what is called the subpoena duces tecum, which must be settled by Judge McDonald's Chamber and which might have an influence on the conduct of the trial, according naturally to what the decision will be. I say for the public, so that it will understand what the schedule for the Blaskic trial will be. We also have pending, and this will be since yesterday -- it is this Trial Chamber which must make that decision which it will do as quickly a possible -- a new decision on the protection of witnesses and a further decision concerning certain measures relating to various depositions. I won't say anything else, because these decisions must be taken by this Trial Chamber, but were discussed in camera yesterday. Lastly, I would like to point out that the Tribunal is faced with a certain number of material constraints. Everybody can see that this courtroom is well equipped. All the conditions have been satisfied here in order to make sure that the trial takes place under the best conditions. Regrettably we have only one trial -- only one courtroom, which we have to share with the other trials that are going on now. The Tribunal is very busy. The three Chambers of the Tribunal are working, the other Trial Chamber as well as the Appeals Chamber, and the Tribunal even had to set up another group of judges for the Celebici trial. Therefore, we will have to operate in sequences, generally two week sequences, and all of this is something which the parties know, but it had to be said in public so that no -- when the interruptions come about, no-one will be surprised. The Tribunal together with the appropriate authorities will have to find a solution so that these physical problems do not have overly great influence on the conduct of this trial. In this respect I have another statement to make. I am talking about the length of the proceedings. I now turn both to the Prosecutor and to the Defence. An international Tribunal wishes to be exemplary and to comply with the highest international standards. All of us in accordance with the covenant on civil rights and the European pact of human rights that we will ensure that General Blaskic enjoys an impartial, fair trial, which takes place within a reasonable time-frame. The proceedings are not completely under the control of the judges. As adopted in the Statute, the proceedings allow a great deal of initiative both to the Prosecution and to the Defence. Both parties know what the judges must take on their own initiative. Nonetheless, turning to the Prosecutor and to the Defence, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman, a great deal of the speed with which this will be carried out will depend both on you, who will determine the number of witnesses that are needed for you to prove, you, the Prosecution, to prove the charges which you have ascribed to General Blaskic, and, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman, to prove your client is innocent. This depends on you. I would like to call your attention to the fact that justice, which is endless, which goes on and on indefinitely, not only would not meet the expectations of international public opinion in civilised countries, but in proper time limits would not respect the right of the trial to have a trial which takes place within a reasonable amount of time. I will say this only one time. I will say it today in public. You cite the number of witnesses that you wish to cite, but I would only like to tell you that the judges of this Tribunal, who have the responsibility of conducting these proceedings under conditions which will guarantee the standards of international justice, and this is their only responsibility, the judges will not hesitate, if necessary, to intervene in order that repetitions and things that would be overly superfluous with the deepest respect for both parties being able to express themselves be taken as much as possible; that is that this not be allowed. If this is not the case, we would only be able to point it out, but at that point each one will be conscious of his own responsibilities. I have no doubt that both parties, with full knowledge that history is looking at us, that we will be judged by posterity, that we very keenly feel the need to make sure that General Blaskic has an impartial, just trial within the trial frame for which he has right and that international public opinion has the right to expect as well. Under these conditions, Prosecutor, I am asking this before even you make your initial charges, that you tell us how you conceive of the conduct, the schedule for the future hearings in terms of how much time you will need in order to prove the guilt, the number of witnesses, according to charges. Are you in a position to do this either today or in the coming days? I will ask the same question of Mr. Hayman. I will conclude by saying that the Tribunal or this Trial Chamber has Judge Shahabuddeen, Judge Riad and myself, who after an election which complies with the Statute of the Tribunal says that I was elected Presiding Judge, I, Claude Jorda. I give the floor to the Prosecution both in order to present your charges and then at the end to say to us how you envisage the conduct of the hearings, because, as I told you, the Tribunal will try to make plans so that the trial takes place under the best conditions and within the best time-frame period possible. I now give you the floor, prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the response to your question about how we intend to proceed will be addressed, if I may seek the court's indulgence in the course of my opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have all the indulgence of the Tribunal, but please do not take advantage of that indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the case over which you and Judge Riad and Judge Shahabuddeen will preside is a case about how Bosnian Croat military forces under the command and control of Tihomir Blaskic ethnically cleansed parts of Central Bosnia in 1993 by systematically attacking Muslim civilians and their homes and destroying their property and by employing methods that no responsible military commander would condone. The illegal methods used by his forces were calculated to achieve an ethnic majority for the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia. The evidence that the Prosecutor's Office will present, your Honours, will show that these illegal methods used by Blaskic's subordinates were widespread over time and area and were well-known to General Blaskic. Indeed, your Honours, they were quite effective. Whole Muslim villages were razed to the ground and their populations were driven from the territory he controlled. Our evidence will show that General Blaskic was a professional soldier who was fully aware of his obligations as a commander under international law, but that he ignored them or was indifferent to them in his determination to achieve Croat domination in Central Bosnia. Let me turn initially to the conflict itself. The former Yugoslavia was comprised of six republics in two autonomous regions, but in the late 1980s and the early 1990s social and political events culminated with the disintegration of that state. Four of the republics, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Macedonia declared their independence. In the wake of those declarations of independence terrible and bloody wars ensued, particularly in Croatia and particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia attempted to deny the peoples of those republics their independence. Now focusing on the war in Bosnia, the parties to the conflict were generally, but not exclusively, divided along ethnic lines: the Bosnian Serbs, under the leadership of Dr Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic sought to cleave out an independent entity known as the Republika Srpska. The socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its army, the JNA, supported this effort, but ultimately international pressure was brought to bear and the JNA was withdrawn, at least nominally from Bosnia on 19th May 1992. In truth and in fact the JNA remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina but merely changed its name. The war machine of the JNA was essentially transferred to the army of the Republika Srpska, the VRS, and throughout the war Belgrade continued to support the VRS with supplies, munitions and armaments. It was possession of these superior arms that gave the Bosnian Serbs a decided advantage at the outset of the conflict in Bosnia. Now opposing the Bosnian Serbs were the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, both groups initially under the direction of the central government, which was located in Sarajevo. Because the Bosnian government was unprepared for war and because of the superior armaments of the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs made impressive territorial gains in Bosnia and seized control over large parts of the country. The Bosnian Croats expressed dissatisfaction with the Bosnian government's weak response to the Serbian aggression, and in 1991 and in 1992 they created the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a quasi-state, and a military component to that state, the HVO, ostensibly for the Defence of Croat interests. Our evidence will show that the Bosnian Croats were provided with significant logistical and manpower support, political direction and diplomatic backing by Croatia in their efforts. While the Bosnian Croats initially allied themselves with the forces of the central government to resist the Serbian offensive, this alliance was short-lived, and shortly it fell apart and a war within a war erupted. That war was the Croat-Muslim war and it is events from that war that occurred in Central Bosnia that are the subject of the second amended indictment before you. Now, to put into context the events of the Croat-Muslim war, I think it's very important to identify the parties to the conflict, their goals and objectives, and the structures of their respective military commands. I will refer during the course of my opening remarks, your Honour, to the military unit of the Bosnian Croats as the HVO and I will refer to the military organisation of the Bosnian Muslims as the Armija. To understand the goals and aspirations of the Bosnian Croats one must initially return to one of the former republics of the former state of Yugoslavia, that is the socialist Republic of Croatia, where in 1988 and in 1989 a new political party was formed. That political party was called the Croatian democratic community or the HDZ. Its leader was Dr Franjo Tudjman, the current President of Croatia, and a well-known former partisan, communist and JNA general. Dr Tudjman drafted the programme of the HDZ, and this programme was nationalistic in tone and asserted, among other things, the right of the Croatian people to self-determination in their historic borders. In April and May of 1990 multi-party elections occurred in Croatia and the HDZ was triumphant. It received the majority of seats in the assembly and on 30th May 1990 the assembled deputies elected Franjo Tudjman as the President of Croatia and Stipe Mesic took the new post of Prime Minister. Following the elections in Croatia, the HDZ political party extended its activities into Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian democratic party of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the HDZ BiH was founded in Sarajevo on 18th August 1990, and it was registered as an "association" in Sarajevo on 6th September 1990. The goals of this Bosnian-Croat party included the right of securing the right of self-determination for Bosnian Croats, the right of secession and the realisation of sovereignty for Bosnia and Herzegovina. The first President of this party was a man by the name of Davor Perinovic, and he was replaced by a man named Stjepan Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic was a moderate Croat, who believed in a single state, a single, multi-ethnic state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our evidence will show that Mr. Kljuic was removed from the head of this party by President Tudjman and ultimately replaced by a man named Mate Boban. I will explain the significance of that event later in my remarks. In November of 1990 the first multi-ethnic elections took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina and resulted in the domination of the nationalist parties: the SDA, which was the Bosnian Muslim party, the SDS, which was the Bosnian Serb party, and the HDZ, which was the Bosnian Croat party. Following these elections, these three parties shared power in the government and the assembly and Alija Izetbegovic, the leader of the SDA party, was named to head the seven member multi-ethnic presidency. Now on 25th June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence and war ensued. The war in Slovenia was over with in ten days, but as the JNA retreated into Croatia, it embarked on a bloody and terrible war. The horrors of war that were visited on Croatia are now permanently evidence in the annals of history and the sufferings of its people in places like Vukovar and elsewhere, and the destruction of its rich cultural heritage shocked the world. It also shocked the Bosnian Croats, many of whom took up arms and went to Croatia in defence of Croatia and their spiritual motherland. While war was raging in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- I'm sorry -- while war was raging in Croatia, the political party of the Bosnian Croats perceived that the Bosnian central government was not robust enough in its dealing with the JNA, which was transiting its troops through Bosnia to the war in Croatia and did not feel they were robust enough in dealing with the Bosnian Serbs, who were acquiring vast swatches of territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This resulted in the establishment of a new entity, a quasi-state known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That was established on 18th November 1991. The capital of this new entry was to be Mostar, and the HZ H-B, this new entity, identified a number of municipalities within Bosnia and Herzegovina that it considered part of the Croatian Community, including incidentally, your Honours, the three municipalities where the crimes alleged in this indictment took place, Vitez municipality, Busovaca municipality, and Kiseljak municipality. The founders of this new entity stated that the Bosnian Croats future was linked to the future of the entire Croat nation and emphasised their own historic responsibility for the Defence of Croatian ethnic and historic territories and the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This new entity's Supreme authority was the presidency and the President of this entity was Mate Boban. Now Mate Boban, Mr. President and your Honours, was a Croat from Herzegovina, who was closely associated with President Tudjman, and he favoured the separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Croats from that republic and their integration into Croatia. In early February of 1992 Stjepan Kljuic, who was the head of the Bosnian Croat political party, was removed from that position at the request of President Tudjman and he was succeeded after a brief hiatus by Mate Boban. Now what was the significance of that? The significance, your Honour, is that it significantly altered the political philosophy of that party. Before the ouster of Kljuic, the party favoured integration of Bosnia's Croats into a single state. With Boban at the helm, the party now sought to meld Bosnian territory into Croatia. The next significant development, your Honours, is that on 8th April, following the start of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presidency of this entity established the Croatian Defence Council, or the HVO, and you will be hearing a lot about the HVO during the course of this trial. The HVO was the military branch of this entity, and General Blaskic was an officer of the HVO. On 13th June 1992 municipal HVOs were established as the municipal executive authorities in Herceg-Bosna, thereby usurping popularly elected local civilian officials. What is especially significant, Mr. President and your Honours, is that this entity rejected a unitary model of state organisation for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the President, Mate Boban, transformed the HVO, the military group, into "the highest body of executive power and administration" in that entry, responsible directly to the presidency. In fact, all authority within this state within a State passed to the HVO, the military body. Thus, a military totalitarian state was created. Now, your Honour, I would like to turn to the command structure of the HVO, and if I could, I would like the ELMO to be turned on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we lower the lights a bit, because there is a glare on the screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the HVO command structure had very clear and direct lines of command and they are illustrated in the piece of paper that I have put on the ELMO. At the top of the command structure was the Supreme commander of the armed forces. That was Mate Boban. Directly subordinate to him, your Honours, was the Ministry of Defence, the head of which was a man by the name of Bruno Stojic. Directly under the Ministry of Defence was the headquarters staff of the HVO. The head officer of that was a man by the name of General Petovic. Then directly under the headquarters staff were four operation zones. Those four operation zones, your Honour, two of them were located in Herzegovina. One of them was located in the north of the country in Posavina. The fourth was located in Central Bosnia and that is where General Blaskic comes into this picture. General Blaskic was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone. Now following this structure down a little bit further, your Honour, you can see that under the operation zone there were operational groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. You said that General Blaskic -- here it says Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. But we are referring to General Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. The ambiguity arises because General Blaskic is currently a General but when he was central Bosnian commander he held the rank of Colonel. Following this structure down the operational zones, there are operational groups. For example, General Blaskic had underneath his operational zone three operational groups, each of which contained a number of brigades centred around the municipalities in which they were located. During the course of this trial you will hear the name of Mario Cerkez, who was a brigade commander in Vitez. You will hear the name of Dusko Grubesic, who was a brigade commander in Busovaca. Thus if you examine this structure, you will see in the HVO hierarchy that General Blaskic was one of the highest ranking members of the HVO and in his theatre of operations he was the highest ranking military commander. I do not need this illustration any further, your Honour. Now, your Honour, how did the HVO work? A central tenant was the principle of unity of command, and that was articulated in a decree on the armed forces, which was promulgated in July of 1992. It imposed two principles. It imposed on subordinates the obligation to implement the decisions and carry out the orders of a superior officer, and it mandated that commanders of the armed forces shall be responsible to their superiors for their work, command and control. Incidentally, your Honours, this decree on the armed forces from July of 1992 also required that military forces in combat operations observe international laws of war, the humane treatment of civilians and prisoners of war, the protection of the population and other protections envisaged in international humanitarian law. Now, your Honours, I would like to briefly turn to the third group in this conflict, the Bosnian Muslims. The government in Bosnia and Herzegovina was led by a Bosnian Muslim, President Alija Izetbegovic, who was the head of the SDA political party. His government sought to achieve a democratically elected, multi-ethnic society, and indeed many Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs supported this concept. Now, when the war start in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was one problem. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have an army. The army, which I will refer to as the Armija, grew up from the remnants of the JNA territorial defence force or the TO, which were essentially local defence courses, which were a component of the JNA and which were part of Tito's all people's defence philosophy. These defence units initially were centred around municipalities, but this structure proved to be not workable in the context of this war, and so the Bosnian Muslims reorganised themselves into a structure consisting of five corps and subordinate brigades. Each of these corps operated in a different area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Supreme commander of the Armija was President Alija Izetbegovic. Now the events that took place in the indictment took place in the area of operation of the III Corps of the Armija. The III Corps was based in Zenica and was commanded by General Enver Hasihasinovic. This area for the III Corps was quite large. It stretched as far north as Tesanj and as far south as Gorni Vakuf and as far east as Sarajevo. It maintained a front line of approximately 400-500 kms against the Serbs. It essentially manned the lengthy spine of what was left of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the start of the war, and it included the strategically and industrially important Lasva Valley, where many of these crimes in this indictment took place. Within the III Corps area of operations was also the Central Bosnia Operation Zone area commanded by General Blaskic. Of the three military forces operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina the Bosnian Muslims were the weakest. That was due to two factors: one, they didn't have regional allies who were willing to supply them with arms, personnel and the like, like Croatia and Serbia, and, secondly, there was an international arms embargo at the time. Consequently, the III Corps and other corps of the Armija were ham-strung by the lack of supplies and, more importantly, a lack of sufficient arms and ammunition. General Hasihasinovic, who will testify in the course of this trial, will say he had approximately 87,000 soldiers in the III Corps area of operation, but only about one-third of them had weapons. For instance in a brigade of about 1200 men, there were only 300-400 weapons that included infantry weapons, machine guns and hunting rifles. So desperate was the situation for the Armija, Mr. President and your Honours, that when a soldier left the front lines, he left his weapon there, so his replacement would have a weapon to fight with. General Hasihasinovic will testify during the course of this year both soldiers carried between 30-50 bullets, some only as few as ten and at one point during the war there was no spare ammunition for his soldiers. With these limitations, your Honour, the Armija struggled to maintain with its Croat allies a 400-500 km front line against their mutual foe, the Serbs. Now, it may be claimed by General Blaskic in the course of this trial, your Honour, that the Armija started the conflict in Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is argument. I object to argument in opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, allow the Judge and the Presiding Judge who are conducting the trial to control things. This is an introductory statement. The Prosecutor is making his statement, basing himself on his charges. Conditioned on what my colleagues may think ... (Pause.) Mr. Hayman, the Tribunal does not accept your intervention. The Prosecution must present what he is presenting. Nonetheless we do ask of the Prosecutor that he attempt as smoothly as possible and without calling into question sources which may give rise to discussion, otherwise we will have further incidents of this type. I say now to the Defence, together with my colleagues, that the Prosecutor here has with the methods that he chooses to use the right to present his accusations. Obviously his statement cannot be a neutral one, as would be that of a Judge. He is explaining all of the charges. If each time that the Prosecutor presents a count or a charge, the Defence will rise and object, I will object to the objections. However, I do ask the Prosecutor, of course, to work in such a way that everything which may give rise to argument may reserved for the portion following his presentation. Thank you. I give you the floor once again, prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I said, your Honour, the evidence that will be presented by the Prosecutor will be that the Armija did not start the conflict in April of 1993 in Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities. It simply is not the case. Under the tenuous and perilous situation that the Armija found itself in with insufficient arms and ammunition, and manning a 400-500 km front line against a very aggressive foe, the Bosnian Serbs, they could ill afford and did not want to have a second front against the HVO. It was against that backdrop that the HVO ratched up the tensions in Central Bosnia that culminated with the events described in the indictment. Now, your Honours, I have identified essentially the parties to the conflict. Now let me turn to General Blaskic and identify him further. General Blaskic was born in Kiseljak municipality in 1992 (sic), one of the municipalities where the crimes alleged in this indictment took place. At the age of 17 he attended secondary school in Belgrade and military academy and was graduated from that, and then went and attended the Academy for Land Forces in Belgrade for four years. While in attendance at that military academy he studied a variety of military subjects, including military law, and he graduated from the Academy in 1983 commissioned with the rank of Second Lieutenant. He was then posted to Slovenia, to Ljubljana, where he taught military studies. He taught reserve officers and military students. In 1987 he was promoted to the rank of Captain and he left the JNA in August of 1991 with a rank of Captain First Class. He went to Vienna. He remained there for a number of months, but then returned to Kiseljak in 1992, where he was appointed Joint Commander of the Armed Forces of the HVO in Kiseljak. He was appointed with a Muslim as a Joint Commander. Both he and the Muslim Joint Commander were subordinates to the Commander of the municipal HVO headquarters in Kiseljak. On 27th June 1992 Mate Boban appointed Tihomir Blaskic as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone. This operation zone initially comprised a number of municipalities, I think approximately 22, but it was later reduced in size. Blaskic thus became one of the most important military figures in the HVO and the highest ranking officer in the Central Bosnia Operation Zone. While he was Central Bosnia Operation Zone Commander he held the rank of Colonel. Later, after the events described in the indictment, he became a Major-General and Chief of Staff of the HVO. In November of 1995, after the indictment was issued, President Tudjman of Croatia appointed him Inspector in the General Inspectorate of the Army of the Republic of Croatia, where he currently holds the rank of General in the Croatian army. The Prosecutor's evidence will show, your Honours, that at all relevant times to the indictment Blaskic was in a position of superior authority to the HVO personnel who committed the crimes described in the indictment. Now, your Honours, I would like to turn to the indictment itself. As I mentioned before I started my opening remarks, there are 20 counts in the indictment, three counts of crimes against humanity; 6 counts of grave breaches of the Geneva conventions; and 11 counts of violations of the laws or customs of war. These counts describe the protracted persecution of Muslims in the Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities by Blaskic and his subordinates. The indictment describes widespread, systematic attacks on largely undefended cities, towns and villages inhabited by Bosnian Muslims, the intentional killing and infliction of serious bodily injury on the Muslim non-combatants, including women, children and the elderly by the HVO; the systematic destruction by fire of Muslim dwellings, of buildings, and of religious institutions by the HVO; the systematic plunder and looting of Muslim property by the HVO; the inhumane treatment of Muslim civilians by the HVO in HVO detention facilities, the systematic use by the HVO of Muslim civilians and in forced labour, including the widespread use digging trenches at front line positions where many of them were killed or seriously injured. Finally, your Honours, it describes the forcible transfer of Muslim civilians by the HVO from their homes and villages. These crimes all occurred in an area of the Central Bosnia operations zone with three small municipalities, which I've previously mentioned. These three municipalities consisted of a narrow area of land stretching essentially the same distance as that between the Hague and Schipol airport to our north. Indeed, Mr. President and your Honours, the crimes described in the indictment, many of them occurred within minutes of Blaskic's headquarters, which were located respectively in the town of Vitez and Kiseljak. For example, the village of Ahmici, where 96 Muslim civilians, women, children and elderly, were murdered by Blaskic's subordinates, and where every Muslim home and both the Mosques were razed to the ground occurred within 5 kms from Blaskic's headquarters in Vitez. That village is visible from the top of Blaskic's headquarters building itself. Stari Vitez, another location about which you will hear in the course of this indictment, where soldiers under Blaskic's command and control committed crimes over an extended period of time, was a mere 300 metres from Blaskic's Vitez headquarters. The Kiseljak barracks, where Blaskic maintained military headquarters, was the location of the detention of numerous Muslim civilians who were from that location taken to the front line positions and forced to dig trenches. Now despite its small area, however, this particular region of Central Bosnia was very important to the Bosnian Croats. It was important because it was relatively close to Herzegovina. It had a large Croat population, because it had an extensive military industrial base and because it sat along strategic lines of communication to Sarajevo. Your Honour, I would like now no turn to Blaskic's responsibility under Articles 7.1 and 7.3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. He is charged under both of those provisions. Under Article 7.1 of the Statute a person who plans, instigates, orders or commits or otherwise aids and abets in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime described in the Statute is individually criminally responsible. Our evidence against Blaskic for 7.1 responsibility for the crimes in the indictment is based primarily on strong circumstantial evidence. First, General Blaskic was a military commander of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone. Second, the uniform methods used by the HVO in committing the crimes alleged in the indictment, particularly within or shortly after the military operations he ordered, included: (a) the systematic burning of Muslim homes and building by flammable liquids or by incendiary ammunition. (b) the systematic looting and plunder of Muslim property 9 (c) the systematic detention of muse limb men and boys. (d) the systematic use of Muslim detainees to dig trenches. (e) the systematic expulsion of Muslims from Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak. (f) and in some villages the systematic killing of Muslim civilians. Third, the pattern and pervasiveness of these methods particularly within or shortly after HVO military operations are strong indications tending to show that Blaskic planned, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of these crimes. This strong circumstantial evidence will be supplemented by evidence that the HVO soldiers who participated in the April 16th attack on the village of Ahmici were given orders to kill Muslim civilians and destroy everything that was Muslim, facts, your Honours, which are sadly reflected on the ground. We have also alleged command responsibility criminal liability. All military commanders have a solemn obligation to ensure that the horrors of war are not visited upon innocent civilians and prisoners of war, and they may be held criminally responsible for this dereliction of duty. As was stated in the case of in Re Yamashita and I quote: "It is evident that the conduct of military operations by troops whose excesses are unrestrained by the orders or efforts of their commander would almost certainly result in violations which the purpose of the law of war is to prevent. Its purpose is to protect the civilian population and prisoners of war from brutality would largely be defeated if the commander of an invading army could with impunity neglect to take reasonable measures for their protection". The principle of command responsibility is enshrined in Article 7.3 of our statutes and holds that a superior is criminally responsible if he knew or had reason to know that a subordinate was about to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down a bit for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I will. I'm sorry. ... was about to commit criminal acts or had done so and failed to take the reasonable or necessary steps to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. To establish this form of criminal liability under the Statute we have to and we will establish the following three elements: 1: The superior concerned must be the superior of that subordinate. Under this element the responsibility of a military commander applies both to the members of the armed forces under his command and to troops who are not normally under his command, but which may be deployed for a particular operation or for a limited period of time. The commander is also responsible to take all possible measures to protect the civilian population against attacks, even if they are not by his direct subordinates, because he is responsible for maintaining law and order in the territory under his de facto control. The second element, your Honour, is that Blaskic knew or had information which should have enabled him to conclude that a breach was being committed, was going to be committed or had been committed. This element may be established either through actual knowledge, established by direct or circumstantial evidence, or through establishing that the accused would have had knowledge were it not for his wilful blindness to the circumstances. Our evidence will show that Blaskic particularly in respect of the attacks that were launched in April that was launched against Ahmici disregarded information at his disposal which indicated a likelihood of criminal offences occurring, and it will show beyond a reasonable doubt that he had actual knowledge, actual knowledge, of all the crimes contained in the indictment. He received that knowledge directly from UNPROFOR soldiers and commanders, from ECMM monitors, from ICRC representatives, from Muslim commanders and through his designated HVO representatives who sat daily on a commission that was established by ECMM designed specifically to hear and to investigate complaints of the parties of the conflict. Additionally, your Honours, the crimes described in the indictment were so widespread as to time and area that they furnished him with abundant constructive knowledge. The third element we must prove in this command responsibility case is that Blaskic failed to take reasonable steps to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators who committed them. Under customary international law a commander is under an obligation to ensure that members of the armed forces under his command are aware of their obligations to abide by the provisions of international law, and he must do so either periodically or expressly before an engagement. We will present some evidence that Blaskic did issue some of these types of orders. However, the mere issuance of routine orders to abide by the Geneva conventions does not relieve a commander of criminal responsibility. His concomitant duty is to ensure that his orders are being effectively carried out. A commander has an affirmative duty to take all necessary measures for the protection of the civilian population. As stated additionally in the Hostage case, and I quote: "The primary responsibility for the prevention and punishment of crimes lie with the commanding general, a responsibility which he cannot escape by denying authority over the perpetrators". Our evidence will show that despite his knowledge of the crimes committed by his subordinates he repeatedly failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to suppress breaches or to punish his subordinates for committing them. His laissez faire attitude encouraged his subordinates to commit crimes. Indeed, instead of punishing his subordinates, he often blamed the Muslims or the Serbs for committing them. Now, your Honours, I would like to turn to the events in the indictment. Background. In the central Bosnian operation zone tensions existed between the two ethnic communities the Croats and the Muslims who were nominally allied against a common enemy, the Serbs. In October 1992 you will hear evidence that there was a brief flare up of fighting in Novi Travnik over possession of an arms factory. Novi Travnik is located next to the town of Vitez. This fighting spilled over in the village of Ahmici, where the Muslims had set up a roadblock, and that roadblock prevented HVO reinforcement from Busovaca being able to go over the hill to Novi Travnik. A brief one-sided fight between the HVO and the few men manning the roadblock ensued, and this resulted in the death of a 17 year old Muslim boy. At the same time these flare-ups were occurring in the Central Bosnia Operation Zone there was fighting between the Muslims and the Croats in Prozor and Gorni Vakuf, areas that were outside the central Bosnian operation zone. In January 1993 another conflict erupted between the HVO and the Muslims, this time in Busovaca. We will present evidence in the form of testimony of the victims of that particular set of events, and they will testify that subordinates of Blaskic attacked them, burned their homes, systematically looted their homes and forced them into forced labour to dig trenches and fortifications for the HVO. In many respects, your Honour, what happened in Busovaca was a dress rehearsal for what was to come later in April. The events that took place in Busovaca and Novi Travnik were brief flare-ups of fighting. While that was happening, the HVO was progressively reducing its role against the Serbs at the front line and concentrating its soldiers in the Lasva Valley in order to prepare for its surprise attacks that occurred in April. Following the two incidents that I have just described in Busovaca and Novi Travnik, strong anti-Muslim sentiment was palpable in the Lasva Valley, particularly in respect of Ahmici, where the HVO felt that it had been obstructed in its fight over the arms factory in Novi Travnik. Throughout the region, and particularly in and around Vitez, discrimination and low-level violence against the Muslim population was constant and unrelenting. For example, Muslims had to swear allegiance to the HVO. If they failed to do so, in some positions they would lose their jobs. Frequently Muslims who had to cross HVO roadblocks to get to their homes and their villages were harassed, and many Muslim shops and businesses that were located around Blaskic's headquarters in Vitez were bombed, firebombed and destroyed. Blaskic was fully aware of this volatile situation and the increasing violence that was being directed against the Muslims when he planned the attacks in April, when he launched his forces on those particular villages that you'll hear about. Now during the time-frame that we've been talking about, that I've been talking about, there was another event that was significant in the events that are described in the indictment. This, your Honour, was occurring in Geneva, where since September of 1992 negotiations involving the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims under the direction of Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen were taking place. The fruit of this effort was known as the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, your Honours, Bosnia and Herzegovina was to become a decentralised state. It was to be divided into ten provinces, each of which was to be controlled by either the Serbs, the Muslims or the Croats. The Croats were assigned three provinces, Provinces 3, 8 and 10. Province number 10 included the Vitez municipality, the Busovaca municipality and part of the Kiseljak municipality where the crimes alleged in this indictment took place. When the Bosnian Croats were shown a map of this territorial division, they were elated. On 4th January 1993 Mate Boban accepted the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in full. He liked the map, the division. However, the Muslims and the Serbs did not. There were further negotiations, and ultimately on 25th March 1993 President Izetbegovic agreed to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan map. However, on 2nd April 1993 the Serbs again rejected the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and the following day Mate Boban said that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan should be implemented. He further stated that if the Bosnian Muslims did not agree to implement the plans of the -- the terms of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan by 15th April, the HVO would move ahead with its implementation. The following day, 16th April 1993, Blaskic's forces launched a devastating series of well-planned and co-ordinated surprise attacks in Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities, those municipalities that were to be included in Province 10 under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. The military operations were meticulously planned military operations. They were supported by artillery and heavy weapons and well-co-ordinated infantry manoeuvres and were not spontaneous eruptions of violence by uncontrollable members outside the HVO chain of command. This is evident, Mr. President and your Honours, by the timing of the attacks which occurred in the three municipalities. In Vitez municipality on 16th April at approximately 5.30 in the morning the HVO simultaneously attacked Vitez, Stari Vitez and the Muslim villages of Ahmici, Nadioici, Santici and Donja Vecerska among others. On 17th April they attacked the village of Loncari and on 20th April they attacked the village of Gacice. In Kiseljak municipality on 18th April 1993 the HVO launched attacks on the Muslim parts of that city, Kiseljak, and on the Muslim villages of Gomionica, Gromiljak, Visnjica, Rotilj, Behrici and Hercizi. On 19th April in Busovaca municipality they attacked Muslim sections of the town of Busovaca and they attacked the village of Ocenici. The evidence that we will present will demonstrate beyond any doubt that the objects of these HVO attacks included Muslim civilians and their property. The crimes described in the indictment were not the work of Muslim extremists or the Serbs, as Blaskic has frequently claimed, nor were they the work of Croat elements not under his control. The crimes described in the indictment were perpetrated by his subordinates, over whom he had command responsibility. Later, in June of 1993, after the tragic events of April, the HVO launched another series of surprise attacks, this time in Kiseljak municipality, and this time against the villages of Han Ploca and Tulica. You will hear the testimony of the victims from those attacks and you will hear them describe the methods that were used by the HVO in those attacks, and they will mirror in many respects the testimony of what you will have previously heard in respect of the April attacks and in respect of the January attack in Busovaca. Now in some of these villages that were attacked in April and June it will be clear from the evidence that there were present in those villages some Armija soldiers, who were home on leave, and some village guard units, generally undermanned and underarmed. This disorganised handful of individuals attempted by whatever means at their disposal to protect themselves, their loved ones and their homes against the HVO onslaught which was directed against them. In the course of their disorganised resistance they inflicted some casualties on the HVO, but in the main, Mr. President and your Honours, the resistance proved futile and their homes, their places of Worship were systematically razed to the ground. You will hear, Mr. President and your Honours, for example, the testimony of Mr. Sakhib Ahmic. Mr. Ahmic will testify in respect of the attack that occurred in the village of Ahmici that occurred on 16th April 1993. Mr. Ahmic is 64 years old. At the time of the attack he was a civilian. He was in his home. Present with him were his son, Naser, Naser's wife and his two grandchildren, Elvis and Sejad. Sejad was three months old. He was listening to the morning prayer coming from the nearby mosque --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the morning recess I was informing the court that there would be the testimony of many victims and you'll be hearing that throughout the course of this trial. I have identified one of those victims by the name of Mr. Sakhib Ahmic. As I was saying, Mr. Ahmic at the time of the attack on the village of Ahmici on 16th April was at home listening to the morning prayer coming from the nearby mosque. In his home was his son, his daughter-in-law and his two grandchildren, one of whom was 3 months old. At the conclusion of the morning prayer there was large explosion at his house and two HVO soldiers entered into his house. The first thing they did was machine-gun to death his son who was standing there without a weapon in his underwear. They then murdered his daughter-in-law. Another HVO soldier took a can of what contained some flammable liquid, perhaps benzine or gasoline and poured it over his couch and ignited it. Subsequently his two grandchildren were murdered. Mr. Ahmic was the sole survivor from this unspeakable attack. His house was razed to the ground, a tactic, Mr. President and your Honours, that you will hear the HVO employed over and over and over again in respect of Muslim houses that are described in many of these villages in this indictment. These crimes, your Honour, in Ahmici were not committed by Muslims trying to embarrass the Croats or by Serbs whose front lines were a significant distance away, as General Blaskic has said, but they were committed by his subordinates. You will hear other victims from other villages from Busovaca, Kiseljak and Vitez and their testimony will in many respects mirror the testimony of Mr. Ahmic's. However, the testimony that we intend to present in the course of this trial will not be limited to Muslim victims. During the course of the events described in the indictment there were independent third parties who were present when these attacks took place or shortly after they occurred. These independent witnesses include Captain Michael Dooley, who was a British officer. He was in Vitez on 16th April as part of the UNPROFOR course. He is a professional soldier. He is currently an instructor at the Royal Military Academy in Sandhurst in Great Britain. He will testify that on the morning of 16th April he went into the town of Vitez in his armoured vehicle and he witnessed the HVO attack in progress and will describe how the HVO is going from house to house systematically attacking houses where civilians were located, and how he was compelled to action at great personal risk to himself and to his men in order to save civilians. Captain Dooley will also testify that on that same day he took his armoured vehicle and went to locations in and around Ahmici and he collected the bodies of 20 or more civilians, mostly women and mostly older folks, and that in his opinion not a single one of those victims that he saw was a combatant. He will testify in his opinion as a professional soldier the attacks were well-organised and well synchronised, and he will testify that in his opinion they were targeted against civilians. In addition to Captain Dooley, Mr. President and your Honours, you will hear the testimony of other independent third parties, including British, Canadian and Dutch UNPROFOR soldiers, who were stationed in the Lasva Valley, members of the ECMM and others. For example, you will hear the testimony of Charles McLeod, an ECMM monitor, a former British officer, who spent a significant amount of time in the former Yugoslavia. After the tragic events that occurred in the Lasva Valley in April, he was sent by the ECMM to the Lasva Valley to conduct an investigation and in the course of that investigation he interviewed a number of people, inspected a number of locations. He even included General Blaskic. He will testify about his investigation and he will testify about his final report, and we will introduce into evidence a copy of that report. Amongst its conclusions are, and I quote: "Croats in Vitez launched a co-ordinated attack against Muslim villages around Vitez". It also includes the conclusion that: "Croats have effectively established a totalitarian regime, having removed any political opposition and established their own combined political/military structure and that they are using extreme measures of terror and genocide to remove the Muslim population and were only prevented from total success by their miscalculation of the Muslim military reaction". Both the testimonies of the victims and the independent third parties will demonstrate a pattern of conduct by the HVO will show that the civilians and civilian targets were targeted through the time-frame and the events described in the indictment. Mr. President and your Honours you will also hear evidence about two indiscriminate HVO attacks which resulted in loss of civilian life. These attacks occurred on 18th April 1993 and 19th April 1993. The first of these attacks involved the detonation of a huge truck bomb in Stari Vitez on 18th April. Now recall, your Honours, that the attack in Vitez started on 16th April, and the HVO in the process of that attack -- many Muslims fled to the old town, the centre, Stari Vitez, in order to defend themselves. There was some presence of soldiers in the Stari Vitez pocket. They fled there for protection and they were defending themselves in that particular area. That's where Captain Dooley, whose testimony I previously referred to, went in with his particular armoured vehicles, you will hear, your Honours, the testimony relating to this truck bombing. What the HVO did on 18th April was they loaded a truck with a huge amount of explosives. It was driven into this town, this part of town and it was detonated. It resulted in massive destruction and significant loss of civilian life and civilian casualties. This event, your Honour, took place a more 400 metres from Blaskic's headquarters. The witnesses who will describe this event will include the survivors of this and will include independent third parties such as Jeffrey Thomas, who was the first British soldier to appear at the scene of this detonation. We will present to you photographs taken by Mr. Thomas and others of this scene. The second indiscriminate attack took place the following day in the city of Zenica. It took place about noon time. It was an artillery attack. It took place at a busy market place in Zenica. This shelling resulted in 15 civilian deaths, 36 civilian casualties, and 18 of them were very, very seriously injured. Present in Zenica at the time of this artillery attack were ECMM monitors who responded to the scene of this artillery attack. They examined the craters, did a crater analysis of what was on the ground and determined that the shells had been fired from HVO -- from the direction of HVO artillery positions. Complaints about both the Stari Vitez bombing and the Zenica shelling were made directly to General Blaskic. His response about the Zenica shelling was similar to what he responded to about Ahmici, that the Serbs did it. Now, Mr. President and your Honours, we will also present evidence that following the January, the April and the June attacks described in the indictment the HVO rounded up non-combatants, usually Muslim men, and took them to HVO detention facilities located in and around Vitez, Busovaca and the Kiseljak municipalities. The justification given was protection of the Muslims themselves and security reasons. There these civilians remained for a period of time ranging from days to many, many, many months. These detention sites included the village -- an entire village, the village of Rotilj, the Kiseljak barracks where Blaskic maintained a headquarter, Kaonik Prison and numerous smaller sites around Blaskic's headquarters in Vitez. It is from these detention centres that hundreds of Muslim civilians were forced to do labour by the HVO. They didn't do it voluntarily. They were taken to the front line by the HVO. They were forced to dig trenches and defensive fortification for the HVO. While they were there they were abused often times. They were subjected to exhausting schedules. They were ill fed and many times they were injured or killed, sometimes by the HVO and sometimes by Muslims across the front lines. The Prosecutor will present evidence that this practice was systematic and was widespread and was employed throughout Blaskic's area of command. Indeed, it was standard operating procedure for the HVO to require Muslim civilians to dig trenches. Blaskic knew about it. He received direct complaints about it. It was a practice that the HVO attempted to conceal from international monitors. Although this widespread practice was illegal, in the eyes of the HVO it was practical and it was practical because the HVO didn't have enough manpower to man its front lines against the Muslims and the manpower sufficient to prepare necessary defensive fortification. Your Honours will also hear evidence from Muslim civilians who were forcibly transferred from their homes by the HVO. Many of these transfers, these forcible transfers, occurred immediately after attacks on the villages I have described. In some instances as many as 200-250 Muslim civilians were essentially taken to an HVO checkpoint and told to get out, walk to Zenica, walk to Muslim occupied territory. They had no choice and often times all they had was the clothes that were on their backs. Once the major violence in these attacks abated the practice of the HVO to expel Muslim civilians from their homes continued. General Blaskic was fully aware of this practice. It was illegal, but he supported it. The practice of population resettlement was a tenant of faith of the HVO and we will present evidence in that respect. Now, your Honours, I would like to turn to the trial itself. As I said in the course of my remarks this morning, the evidence that we will present will primarily be witness testimony. Because the indictment alleges crimes that are perpetrated against civilians and civilian objects over a considerable period of time and because it occurred in three municipalities and the city of Zenica, it will not be possible to capture all of the specific criminal acts alleged in the indictment with only a handful of witnesses. Despite the large number of witnesses we intend to present, we will endeavour to move through the testimony with all the speed that justice requires. We will also present, Mr. President and your Honours, photographs, video tapes and maps relating to many of the locations that are described in the indictment. We will also present many orders that were issued by General Blaskic while he was the Central Bosnia operations zone commander, including orders to attack villages that are mentioned in the current indictment, as well as some orders of General Blaskic instructing his subordinates to follow international law, and also to make enquiry into events that occurred after the Ahmici event. However, we do not have a complete set of those orders. We have been endeavouring since 15th January to obtain them from the HVO archives and we have been obstructed in our efforts to obtain a complete set, and therefore we will be unable to furnish the Trial Chamber with a complete set of those orders. We will also present numerous statements of Blaskic, including his many denials of responsibility. Naturally, Mr. President and your Honours, we would like to present all of our witnesses in logical order, but because of the current trial schedule, because of the schedules of some of the witnesses and because we have witnesses who are all over the world, it will not in every case be possible to do so. Therefore, at times we will have to present some of our witnesses out of order. While we unhappily accept this reality, we will endeavour to minimise this problem, whenever possible. In conclusion, Mr. President and your Honours, we will present evidence sufficient to convict Blaskic on all counts of the indictment. That concludes my submissions, your Honours. Thank you very much.
