utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Can you tell us when it was submitted to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. One moment, please. (Pause.) If your Honour wants to take a break, we will send our assistant up to get the letter that was sent to counsel concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The Tribunal is going to suspend the hearing for a few minutes. I must say quite frankly that the Tribunal is here to ensure equality of conditions. I'm referring to the Defence. If this witness was not communicated to the Defence, then the Defence must have his right to cross examination. In those conditions we will hear the witness and then he will remain at the disposal of the Defence for a day or two to give them time to organise themselves. On the other hand, the judges will not allow every time these problems of communication to occur. Therefore we will resume at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, have you found the document which would demonstrate that you had disclosed the name to the Defence? Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. On a letter of 2nd May 1997 a letter signed by Mr. Harmon was sent to Mr. Nobilo and also a letter was sent to Mr. Hayman, where Mr. Donia's name was listed as an expert witness. He is listed as an expert witness at the request of Mr. Hayman, albeit his name is misspelt and there is an "R" in there as opposed to just "N-I-A" but he has been listed as number 95. With regard to the communication that it was received, it was sent by an airway bill by Sky Net and we have the airway bill number if the Tribunal so desires where the actual number that was sent to both counsel is in our possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, some brief explanations before we hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We received this letter, your Honour, and there is no Mr. Donia on the letter. I understand the witness' name, and I understand this only from the spoken words of the Prosecutor this morning, is spelt "D-O-N-I-A". I would ask that the Prosecutor tender a copy of this letter to the court, because there is no person by that name on the letter. If I understand him properly, there is a person named Dornia, D-O-R-N-I-A. The Prosecution has been given the names of approximately 300 witnesses and where there is no witness statement, and in the case of this Mr. Donia there was no witness statement, we have no other information upon which to identify the person. I can represent my office went to great lengths to try to locate and identify Mr. Donia, Robert Donia. We were unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Were there any other consequent indications which would have given further details? Perhaps you could show this to the Tribunal. Perhaps we could put it on the projector, in fact, so that the Trial Chamber could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I will give to the usher is the letters to Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman. Likewise there are the airway bills. The relevant name is on 55 "Donia". As I said at the outset it is misspelt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were there any other things aside from that error, the spelling mistake? In countries which languages you do not speak, therefore there could be mistakes in spelling. Were there any other things that would have allowed the Defence to find this Mr. Donia or was there only the name that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The name was given as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where is the name? Oh, yes, Robert Donia. 55; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Robert Donia, expert witness. With that, Mr. Hayman, you were unable to find this person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were unable, your Honour, because when we're given a name, a person who can be anywhere in the world, the only way to find such a person is through the use of computers to search for articles, speeches, books, and computers are very literal, as your Honours are aware, and if I do not have the right spelling of the name, then I cannot identify the witness. We did not identify this witness. If this witness is truly an expert, I am sure he has given speeches, he has written articles, he has written books perhaps. We have none of those articles. I have no materials. I have been able to obtain no materials concerning this individual. So I would say two things, your Honour. May I? One, we have been prejudiced in that we cannot prepare for this individual, and so forth. Secondly, this individual should not be and cannot be allowed to testify, period, not today, not tomorrow, not next month. Rule 67A(i) provides: "As early as reasonably practicable and in any event" and I repeat "and in any event" "prior to the commencement of the trial the Prosecutor shall notify the Defence of the names of the witnesses that he intends to call". This witness was known to the Prosecution before the commencement of trial and was not notified -- the person's name was not given, was not notified to the Defence. The reason we ask for this sanction is there has to be a sanction or else there is no reason for the rule. I would also submit that under the court' decision under production materials rendered on 27th January 1997 the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecutor -- this is in paragraph 56 -- to disclose to the Defence the names of the witnesses which he intends to call at trial by 1st February 1997 "at the latest". I do not take issue that they may have identified this individual after February 1st, but I submit that the order and Rule 67, taken together, this witness cannot be allowed to testify. It would violate the rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I believe that the Tribunal is as concerned as you are about respecting the Rules. Nonetheless the Tribunal considers that the fair procedures which you must benefit from must be looked at as a whole when it comes to all of the formalities that are required. Therefore I have a question that I would like to ask you: when you were unable to find this Robert Dornia or Donia, did you say to the Prosecution you did not find the name or any trace of this witness? Can you demonstrate to us that you contacted the Prosecution about this issue or did you simply say: "I do not find it. Therefore it doesn't exist". If that was the case I could say that you yourself really opened yourself to criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have sent the Prosecution many letters asking for many clarifications and responses on discovery issues. In the past few months virtually none of those letters have been responded to. There are other expert witnesses that we have not been able to identify, but when your letters are not responded to, with all due respect to the court, at one point -- at a certain point you stop writing letters. It's a futile exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Talking about futile exercises, you know that for months now we have been trying to settle this issue of disclosure. The Tribunal can do many things. It cannot force the parties to come to an agreement about the best methods of communicating with one another. With my colleagues I am going to consult at the bench in order to come to a decision as to what the best thing to do would be. (Pause.) The Tribunal has deliberated on the issue and notes that this is a significant error, a material error, and also considers that it must be sure that both the Defence and the Prosecutor have equal arms. In this case there was no imbalance of arms, at least so long as we have not heard the witness and so long as the Defence has not been able to cross-examine. However, the Tribunal will not give up on hearing the witness since there was an error and decides he will be heard on 30th June, Monday, in the morning. Turning to the Prosecutor, do you have a different witness or another witness you would like to introduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I do not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you have another witness for tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I do not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were you assuming that this -- how long were you expecting this witness to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Depending on cross-examination, your Honour, almost the balance of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This morning I said that the trial should move as quickly as reasonably possible. I believe that the Prosecutor must always have in reserve so that when there is an intervention by the defence that the Prosecutor has a certain number of witnesses in reserve in order to ward off the problems that are of this type or more serious ones. (Pause.) The Tribunal will not countenance any delays. We will now hear the expert witness. The cross-examination will be postponed until Monday morning. You can bring the witness in. (Witness enters court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are before the international Tribunal, sir, the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. You agreed to testify for the Prosecution. I would like to tell you that before you came into the courtroom there was an incident which means -- which derives from the fact that your name was incorrectly spelt and was not able to be given to the Defence. The trial must move forward, however, and therefore we have decided we would hear you today as long as necessary questioned only by the Prosecutor and when the Defence will be ready, we consider that could be for next Monday. If the Defence are not ready, we would postpone it further but then you would be asked to return to The Hague in order to be questioned by the Defence. You may read the solemn declaration which was given to you, sir. First of all, did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for listening to me and understanding my language. Mr. Dornia, first of all we would ask you to spell your name, because apparently this is the origin of the problem. Could you please spell your name for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is Robert J Donia. First name R-O-B-E-R-T, middle initial J, last name D-O-N-I-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So it is Donia, not Dornia, but Donia. Excuse me, sir. Donia. Now we all know it's Donia. There's no "R"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please read the declaration which was given to you, which must be done before the Trial Chamber MR. ROBERT DONIA (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President and your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, prior to beginning with Mr. Donia, I would just ask for a redaction. (Pause.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The Tribunal will order the redaction of the document that was shown. Very well. Having regulated almost all the incidents, Mr. Robert Donia can answer the questions of Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can you tell us what you do for a living at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm in the financial services industry. I am a manager with the firm of Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long have you been so employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During your career prior to Merrill Lynch and to the present time, sir, have you been involved and have you studied as a historian focusing on the affairs in south-east Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give the court a general view of your background in the area, some of the publications that you have authored as well as articles, if you have authored the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1972 until 1976 I pursued a PhD degree in history at the University of Michigan, specialising in the history of South-Eastern Europe and Bosnia in particular. In 1974-1975, with the assistance of a Fullbright research grant, I conducted research in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina and various other archives pertaining to the area and completed a dissertation in 1976 dealing with the Bosnian Muslims in the period of Austro-Hungarian administration around the turn of the century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the title of the dissertation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The dissertation was subsequently published as a book under the title "Islam under the Double Eagle: The Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1878-1914".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I subsequently did additional research in the late 1970s prior to leaving the academic world and more recently, beginning in 1992, worked with my former mentor at the University of Michigan, John Fine, on a book entitled "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When was that published, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was published in 1994 by Colombia University Press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also was able to conduct various interviews and do additional research concerning the contemporary period, that is the 1990s, and wrote articles dealing with the cities of Mostar and Tuzla in the publication "Transition" put out in Prague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to the book you published, "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed", can you tell the Tribunal basically the subject matter of that book and what you and Professor Fine were trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was no single available volume which summarised the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was our intent to produce an interpretative history of Bosnia, focusing on recent events but exploring their origins from the 6th century onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What portion of that book were you responsible for and what portion of that book was Professor Fine responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote the modern period 1878 to present. Professor Fine wrote the section from the 6th century up to 1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you said you published this book in 1994. During that time and since that time have you stayed involved in affairs in Bosnia specifically and have you travelled to that area to keep yourself abreast with events?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for interpretation, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise again to the interpretation booth. Since the publication of that book have you continued to stay involved in the affairs especially in Bosnia and have you continued to travel to that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since the book appeared in November of 1994 I have made seven trips to Bosnia, an additional one only to Croatia and have maintained contacts with professional colleagues, done interviewing and generally explored various contemporary and historical topics in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you continued to stay involved with any academic institutions in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the University of Sarajevo and the Institute for History in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time with Mr. Donia's background and the history of former Yugoslavia, we would move ahead with the presentation of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I interject, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting, but I feel it is necessary. The witness is reading from some kind of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The witness is reading from some kind of a document and I would ask that it be provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman. You are right. Mr. Donia, would you be kind enough not to read documents, otherwise the Defence will have to be supplied with the document. Either that document should be provided for the Defence or avoid referring to it. Which do you prefer, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, if I'm not mistaken, nothing Mr. Donia has said to this point has referenced any document before him. He has been talking about his historical background. He does attempt to refer to a rather brief outline, which is not a statement in any way, shape or form. We'll gladly offer that to the Defence. It's in outline form. It's not a statement. If counsel for the Defence wants it, certainly he can have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The document will be given to the Defence and you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just get the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As you see, the document is being supplied to you very quickly, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue with or without a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I do want to say at this point that this is nothing more than an outline of Mr. Donia's evidence. It is not a statement, etc., so we give it to the Defence counsel with those caveats in mind, and we tell the court the same. Mr. Donia, in the preparation for your testimony here today did you prepare an outline for the review of the court as well as a chronology of some pertinent events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Those are entitled "ICTY presentation outline" and "Lands of the western Balkans chronology".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time for the court's purposes I would give to the court in English and French copies of the outline as well as the chronology that is appended thereto?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, the witness is here presumably to deliver oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but I see no problem in a document being provided by the Prosecution. We are impartial and neutral and when you yourself have a witness, I can promise that should you wish to provide a document to the Tribunal, you will be allowed to do so. Therefore, we will admit this document, Mr. Hayman. Can we allow the presentation to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I state my position, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may state your position, but it is rather regrettable that it should be stated after the statement of the Trial Chamber, but, as I interrupted you, you may continue with your reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm concerned that if it's solely an outline for the witness' use, that's one thing. The Prosecution has taken the position it's not a statement. It's for the witness' use. So it was not provided to the Prosecution in discovery as a statement pursuant to the court's order of January 27th. Yet now it is being tendered to the court presumably as a form of written testimony. If not written testimony, then something that will help the court take in the testimony of this witness. It is 19 pages long. So as a matter of procedure I'm happy to proceed, I'm happy for the Trial Chamber to have this document, but I request that before this procedure is attempted again by the Prosecution, I have an opportunity to address it with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's an entirely different document. Counsel is objecting to a document he has not even seen. What Mr. Donia -- and the exhibit that we have just presented to the usher is a one-page outline and a chronology. Not a 19 page outline that we do not intend to introduce into evidence but that I gave to counsel. They are entirely two different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Just a moment. Let's establish some order. Listen to me. What kind of a document is the one that you are submitting to the Tribunal? I want to see it. Thank you. Very well. This is a document which, if I have well understood, goes in support of the oral statement of the witness; is that correct, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I do not see why the Tribunal should not have a document of one of the parties when it can also be provided to the Defence. It is up to you not to accept that document. As far as the Tribunal is concerned, it will accept it and it will act in the same way with regard to documents that some of your witnesses may have. The incident being closed, I propose that we continue -- we have another ten minutes -- and that we really begin with the questioning of Mr. Robert Donia by the Prosecution. You have the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Donia, in preparation of the writing of your book and subsequently, have you had occasion to take a look at the catastrophic events that caused the break-up of the former Yugoslavia from the late 1980s up until virtually the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you had occasion during those studies as part of your studies to look at the convergence of events that led to the conflict between the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims that took place in large part in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your historical background and being a historian, do you see in the past history, both recent past and distant past, certain items which lead you up to this point to make some conclusions as to how certain events took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the past several centuries are very relevant to what occurred in that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your own words, Mr. Donia, could you explain to the Tribunal your starting point, what you need to go back in history to explain how certain events took place and your conclusiary remarks. During this period of time, your Honour, we will be using the ELMO, because Mr. Donia does have some maps that he would like to display.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would like to begin by presenting a map of Yugoslavia as it existed in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I think that we have established the Rules of order. I wish us to progress. I should like to remind you that the Tribunal is entitled to familiarise itself with all the elements. I will give you the floor just one more time. I'm listening to you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I ask on behalf of the Defence that before the witness refers to documents that the document be shown to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, we just took a decision that you are entitled to make your cross-examination under conditions that will be on an equal footing next Monday, if you wish in July, August or whenever you will. The witness will come back. That's the guarantee that the Tribunal has given you. It cannot give you any others. On the other hand, the Tribunal wishes to hear this witness. During your cross-examination you will be entitled to all the documents that the Tribunal has. That, in my view, is a just and equitable proceeding common to Common Law and civil law systems. We will discount the time we have spent on incidents so we can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Donia begins, I would ask that the map that has been put on the ELMO be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will continue until 1.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map represents the six republics of Yugoslavia as they existed largely unchanged from the period 1945-1990. Those six republics are Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia with its attached autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, and Macedonia. In these six republics in the year 1990 the first multi-party elections were held since World War II. These elections turned out to be a centre point of change for the elections brought nationalist leaders to power in all six of the republics. In Bosnia-Herzegovina those elections took place in November of 1990 and likewise brought nationalist leaders to power. Those nationalist leaders were represented by three parties. For the Muslims the leading party was the party of Democratic Action -- in its native acronym SDA -- which won 86 seats out of the 240 seats in the representative assembly; for the Serbs the group was -- the party was the Serbian Democratic Party, known as the SDS, which won 72 seats; for the Croats of Bosnia, the Croatian Democratic Union, known as the HDZ, which won 44 seats. Of the remaining 38 seats, they were shared by eight different political groups. This represented a major transition, because prior to this time socialism and a single party had prevailed in Yugoslavia, and afterwards and indeed to this day nationalist leaders have prevailed in the region and in Bosnia itself. It represented the defeat of the reformists, reformed socialists and communists, who were defeated in all major areas of the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia with the exception of a few cities. Principal among them is the city of Tuzla in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, this location right here, which to this day remains under a coalition of parties committed to multi-ethnic government. The election of 1990 was a centre point of change, and I would like to use it as a point from which to look backward and then, as I return to it, look forward from the events of 1990 to those of 1993. Immediately after the election of 1990 a census was taken in 1991, and I would like to share the physical map which shows the result of that census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me have this marked, your Honour, before Mr. Donia begins. There are, of course, copies for your Honour as well as the witness and the Defence. If I could ask the usher if we could possibly put this particular ethnic census map on the clip board.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The results of the elections of 1990 and the census of 1991 largely mirrored one another, that is in each instance you can see the highlighting of the ethnic or national groups in certain areas, but largely mixed returns throughout the entire province of -- republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, may I interrupt. Your Honour, if I may, the usher is going to give Mr. Donia some headphones with a longer wire so he can address the map itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fine. I think I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you do it from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are simply two points to be made from this. Number 1, on this map the yellow areas are truly mixed ethnic regions. The map, therefore, is ethnically a very complex one. This is not a land which can be simply divided along mountain ranges or rivers into ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, when you say mixed ethnic groups, can you tell us what those ethnic groups are that are mixed in that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the groups are fundamentally the same. They voted that way in the 1990 elections, namely the Serbs, the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, who have recently adopted the name of Bosniaks. There are a few areas which approach the 100 per cent area for a single ethnic group. Principally this region to the east and south of Mostar, which is heavily of Croatian population. There are some areas of the north which have substantial concentrations of Serbs and a pocket around the city of Bijaz, north of the city of Bijaz, which is largely Muslim. The cities are the most mixed parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1991 census. These circles here represent the population of the major Metropolitan areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some have a Muslim majority population represented in green, but most have a combination of Muslims, Serbs represented in the pink or red, and Croats, represented in blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you begin, you are pointing to the left side of the map where there are certain circles which depict geographical locations and the respective ethnic composition of those locations, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are the ethnic compositions of the major cities and they are identified as such on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such a mixture of population as reflected in the 1991 census is the result of several different developments over many different centuries, and I would like to go back to early times and promise to return with all deliberate speed to the 20th century, arriving back here so we can move forward from 1990 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How did we get there? The easiest and most facile explanation for Bosnia's history came to the surface in 1991. It was the notion that these people are animated by ancient tribal hatreds. This notion suggests that all peoples of the region are primitive and violence prone. They are filled with primordial hatred for one another. Animosity towards their neighbours is deeply embedded in the souls and psyches of all South Slavs. Such an interpretation sees recent events or the violence that characterised this region in World War II as inevitable, as a result of people's fundamental human nature in the area, and sees such events as sporadic, periodic outbursts of violence that could in no way be arrested by outside intervention. Thus there developed a kind of a linkage between this view of ancient tribal hatreds and the policy viewpoint of those statesmen who wanted to avoid any kind of engagement in the Balkan crisis. In fact, this viewpoint was promulgated by Western political leaders to distance themselves from events in Bosnia. In fact, the ancient tribal hatreds viewpoint has no identifiable foundation in the historical understanding of any South Slavs group of its own origins. Each group, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, has an understanding of its past that highlights past accomplishments and long periods of perceived oppression by other groups but no group postulates the notion that there has been this kind of mutual slaughter over many centuries. In fact, the South Slavs migrants essentially lost their tribal character by the end of the Middle Ages, so to speak of tribal hatreds is indeed inappropriate from about the 12th or 13th century onward. One will see in this brief account occasional violence and contention at many points in time, but to suggest that that contention is ethnic, tribal or religious until the 20th century is to mistake the nature of the development of the South Slavs peoples. The origin of the South Slavs in the Balkan Peninsula dates back to the 6th or 7th centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Donia, and we will turn to another exhibit which we would like to hand to the usher. May I proceed, Mr. President? Mr. Donia, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map, which is from a recent atlas of historical maps regarding Eastern Europe, shows the homeland of the South Slavs in the area where present day north-western Ukraine, south-western Belarus and eastern Poland come together. The map shows that there is substantial disagreement amongst scholars about the exact area of the origins of this migration, and indeed the people who made this migration at the time could not write and left no written records. There is substantial agreement that the South Slavs migrated to the Balkan peninsula as tribes. Unlike the Huns and Visigoths and Avars and later the Mongols, these Slavs were sedentary peoples and once they reached the Balkan peninsula after some period of time they settled down and indeed have not migrated as groups since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again this migration occurs during what time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the 6th-7th centuries. Some scholars would put it as late as the 8th but I think it is safe to say that 6th-7th centuries are dates most scholars would accept for this migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they arrived in the Balkan Peninsula there were two rival centres of Christendom, one in Rome and one in Constantinople. Consequently the South Slavs were Christianised from two directions by two different types of influences, from the west by Roman Catholicism and from the east by Orthodox Christianity. Most important in the orthodox missions was that of Cyril and Methodius, which I have noted on the chronology, usually dated 863. Cyril and Methodius were two missionaries who passed through the South Slavs lands and are credited with developing the Cyrillic script, which came to be the basis for modern day Russian and the language of Serbian. There was indeed one Christian church before the year 1054, but these two variants which ultimately resulted in a break in that year meant that the South Slavs from this time forward were really members of two different cultures, Roman Catholicism to the west and Orthodoxy to the east. Starting in about the 9th century there was a period in which Balkan States emerged. This was a time when there were very many rival empires in the area, the Byzantine empire based in Constantinople, the Francs based in Western Europe and some time later during the period Venice, located at the top of the Adriatic Sea. But within this context over time, over the next several centuries, three empires or three kingdoms significant to our enquiry came about, that is of the Bosnian, the Croats and the Serbs. Remarkably little is known about these states and, in fact, the evidence is largely from outsiders, missions that came to the area, occasional royal charters, some archeological evidence, but to our dismay we know very little about these empires compared to what we would like to know. They have probably assumed more significance in the 20th century than they did in the 10th, because current nationalist populisers have turned to them as the basis for their own nationalist claims. These were essentially rulers of tribes and tribal confederations who were seeking to enhance their own power through armed retinues, systems of taxation, conquest, coinage, particularly in the Serbian case the endowment of churches and monasteries, and through acquiring elevated titles, Duke and King and so on. They were highly dependent upon the effectiveness of a single ruler or succession of rulers. I would like to share with you a few maps of this area, but I would also preface that by saying that maps in many respects are inappropriate because they emphasise too much the degree of control that may have existed at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The extent of these rulers' control over territory was often limited to their ability to control vassals, to extract taxation and was often transient in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How was that extent of power of these respective kingdoms of significance to events post-1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly led many people to ascribe to these entities a grandeur that they did not possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you going to move to that next map at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can give the next map to the usher, your Honour. Turning to the next exhibit, Mr. Donia, can you explain that please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of the Medieval Bosnian state. It shows the progressive growth of that state from a small island in what is today Central Bosnia, expanding to the east, to the Drina river and down to the Adriatic coast, and then encompassing much of Dalmatia and going up into the area that is again present day Bosnia. The Bosnian state emerged from Hungary and overlordship in 1180, although it remained nominally under Hungarian control through most of the Middle Ages. The first leader of this state was Ban Kulin. "Ban" is the title that the South Slavs used for a governor, and in at that time it was limited to the small circle that we drew earlier. A successor of Kulin's, Kotromanic, conquered much of the southern region from the Nemanji dynasty, which was the Serbian king, and the rein of King Trvtko, which I have noted on the chronology as well, which ended in 1391, was the point at which this entire state came under his overall control. Trvtko was crowned the King of Bosnia and Serbia in 1377 and in 1390 he added Croatia and Dalmatia to his rein and to his crown. Now that was followed by pressure from the emerging Ottoman Empire and Hungary, which ultimately led to the Ottoman conquest of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question with regard to this. So the outline that you have just encircled with your pointer was essentially the high watermark of the Bosnian empire going back to 1390, when it annexed Croatia and Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. To be clear, it annexed Croatia. It did not annex all of the Dalmatian area, just the coastal region. As important as the State itself was its religious history. Hungary, the kingdom to the north, wanted to conquer and retain this area as part of its crown and developed the accusation that there was a widespread heresy in Bosnia, a dualist heresy known as Bogomilism. This caused the Bosnians to break with the Catholic Church and establish their own independent church known as the Medieval Bosnian Church. This church existed right on the fault line between Catholicism and Orthodoxy and was widely believed by outsiders to be a haven for these Bogomil heretics. Recent scholarship has strongly challenged this assumption, but the Bogomils have come to be seen by the Bosnian Muslim nationalist leaders as the forerunners of the Islamic community, the group of Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In fact, the Franciscan Mission to Bosnia was established in the year 1342 under the sponsorship of the Ban, and thereafter Medieval Bosnia was increasingly catholicised, but for this roughly 100 years from 1252-1342 the Medieval Bosnian Church flourished in much of Bosnia-Herzegovina and came to play an important role in the discussions about the origins of Bosnian peoples after 1990. In 1347 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Donia. We are about to conclude for this morning. I just didn't wish to interrupt you in the middle of your presentation if you need two or three more minutes, but we would not like the Prosecutor to ask any more questions now. Can we stop now, Mr. Donia, or do you have a few more presentations to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The demise of the Bosnian church is an ideal time to stop the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Continue then up to that point, if you wish. Do you wish to continue or do you prefer that we stop here? In that case the meeting is adjourned until tomorrow at 10.00 am. (1.20 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
